turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. How have you been getting on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I am thirty weeks pregnant, and I have come because of a creeping feeling in my legs at night. I am not sleeping with it.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're very welcome. Thirty weeks, fair play to you. Tell me about these legs, in your own time.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, once I lie down they begin to creep, as if something were crawling under the skin. I have to get up and walk about the room. It is every night, though I am not entirely sure when it began, perhaps three weeks.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can vouch for that, doctor. I hear her pacing the landing most nights, and she is wrecked the next day.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the sleep itself, how has that been for you?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I am awake for a good part of every night. By the afternoon I feel like a wet rag.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is there anything else on top of that, or is it mainly the legs?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, my feet feel dead when I am in bed, a numb feeling in both of them. And these past few days there is a frog in my throat. It is only mild.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): A frog in the throat, right. Is there any pain when you swallow, or just that feeling?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No pain, doctor. Just that feeling, and it is mild.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you still at work through all this?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I teach junior infants. By three o'clock I can't hear myself think with the noise in the classroom, and I do feel I have overdone it.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We were nearly late in, doctor. The rain coming from Lucan was lashing, and the M50 was stopped dead.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't doubt it for a minute. It has been pouring since early on. Did ye catch any of the hurling? My brother was up in Croker and he said the pitch was pure muck.
[SEG0016] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We had a bit of it on in the waiting room. Sure it was a grand match until the rain came sideways again. I was perished in the car the whole way.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, you'd want the heavy coat today. Right. Any swelling in the ankles or the calves during the day?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, doctor. There is no swelling.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any headache, or little spots in front of the eyes?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have had neither.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): And how about the chest. Any shortness of breath, or pain there?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. My breathing is perfectly fine, and there is no pain.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand. What medicines are you taking at the minute?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, I take folic acid, four hundred micrograms, by mouth, every morning, for the pregnancy. And the iron tablet, galfar I think they call it, three hundred and five milligrams, once a day by mouth, which the midwife gave me for the low ferritin.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Galfer, yes, that is the ferrous fumarate. Do you remember what the ferritin came back as?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, doctor. They told me it was eleven, about a month ago. I have taken the tablet every day since.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else at all?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have no allergies that I am aware of.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at the legs now. Mm. The calves are soft, there is no swelling, and the pulses in the feet are grand.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Your blood pressure today is one hundred and twelve over 68, and the pulse is eighty-four. Both are lovely.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think what you are describing is restless legs. It is very common at this stage, and with the ferritin having been low it may well be tied in with that. I would not call it definite until we see the new bloods.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll book a ferritin blood test at the desk today. Keep going with the folic acid and the Galfer. A warm bath before bed, and a short walk when the creeping starts, can take the edge off it.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I should mention that the midwife check is already booked for next Wednesday.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Perfect. We'll leave that midwife visit planned for next Wednesday. And if the creeping is still bad after the bloods, come back in to me and we will have another look.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I am very grateful, doctor. I shall do exactly as you say.

spec.situation: Pregnant woman at 30 weeks with creeping legs at night and poor sleep; ferritin discussed; takes folic acid and iron; midwife check booked.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
